cases.task: An Indian ad frame with a Hindi headline.

input.label: The brief
input.text: A dawn chai stall, steam rising — the board should read सुबह की पहली चाय (“the first tea of the morning”).

candidates.note: Reads सुबह की पहली चाय — letter-perfect.
Gorgeous scene — but the Devanagari is nonsense.

cases.verdict: One board reads सुबह की पहली चाय, letter-perfect. One reads gibberish dressed up as Hindi. Both look the part — only one is safe to put in front of a customer.
cases.convert: If you picked the prettier frame, so would most people — that’s the trap. It got the Hindi wrong. Beautiful doesn’t matter if the words don’t; the one worth sending is the one your customer can actually read.

cases.task: Which one actually looks like India?

input.label: The brief
input.text: A crowded Mumbai local at rush hour in the monsoon — humid window light, commuters packed close, candid documentary photograph.

candidates.tag: Nails India · the one worth sending

cases.verdict: No loser here — both are unmistakably India. When two outputs are this close, the one worth sending is the one that costs less to make.

aight.label: What Aight assembles
aight.mechanism: scene generated, headline composited on top

cases.verdict: A base model paints the sign into the scene — and gets the Hindi wrong (it wrote सुवह, not सुबह). Aight generates the scene clean and composites the headline as its own layer — so सुबह की पहली चाय stays razor-sharp and correct on every frame. Text is a layer, not a gamble.
